intent_synonyms: how to distinguish speakers|write different voices|everyone sounds alike
model_instruction: Establish each speaker's status, emotion and relationship before assigning vocabulary, sentence length and subtext; changing names is not enough.
summary: Differentiate voices through diction, sentence length, tone and subtext rather than giving everyone the same formal register.
details: Keep differences consistent in politeness, sentence length, verbal habits, attacks and evasions.
applicable_scenes: Sustained ensemble dialogue, confrontation, probing conversations
pitfalls: Everyone speaks identical polished sentences with different forms of address.
positive_example: “Get to the point.” He tapped the table. “If you will hear me out, sir, I can explain,” she replied evenly.
negative_example: “Get to the point,” he said. “If you will hear me out, sir, I can explain,” she said. Both sound like the same narrator.

intent_synonyms: how to write feelings|inner life|emotional scenes
model_instruction: Show the trigger and bodily reaction before conscious interpretation; avoid circular introspection and piles of abstract labels.
summary: Link the trigger, physical response and interpretation instead of naming an emotion alone.
details: Move from event to subtle reaction to interpretation to action, making the inner change perceptible and consequential.
applicable_scenes: Emotional scenes, setbacks, changes of mind, relationship development
pitfalls: “He was sad” or “She was angry” with no cause or manifestation.
positive_example: Only when the door closed did he notice his wet palms. The explanation he had rehearsed lodged in his throat.
negative_example: He felt terribly sad, hurt and conflicted, full of complicated emotions.

intent_synonyms: how to make scenes vivid|describe setting without dragging
model_instruction: Keep only sensory information useful to the scene; make the environment serve action, emotion and conflict.
summary: A few distinctive sensory details establish a scene better than static adjective lists.
details: Prioritize sights, sounds and textures relevant to the conflict; environmental changes can echo the character's state.
applicable_scenes: Pre-battle tension, emotional atmosphere, opening a transition
pitfalls: Using every sense and flourish at once brings the story to a halt.
positive_example: Wind rattled the corridor lamps. She said nothing, but tightened her grip on the sword.
negative_example: The night was dark, the sky dark, the wind cold, the air cold: atmosphere without movement.

keywords: pressure and release|pacing tension|stored pressure|payoff delivery
intent_synonyms: how to deliver an explosive payoff|build frustration first|pace a breakthrough
model_instruction: Accumulate real restrictions and emotion before releasing them; the breakthrough must fulfill earlier promises.
summary: Build pressure, break the deadlock, then pay it off so the reader's frustration feels worthwhile.
details: Explain why the protagonist cannot act yet; the release should recover setup, reverse relationships and change the situation, not merely announce victory.
pitfalls: Restrictions are artificial or the release fails to fulfill the setup.
positive_example: He endured three trials without defending himself. Only when the elder moved to revoke his place did he reveal the token. The hall fell silent.
negative_example: With no earlier pressure, a sudden great victory has no satisfying contrast.

intent_synonyms: how to cut small talk|dialogue says nothing|make dialogue matter
model_instruction: Remove greetings that change neither plot nor relationships; focus speech on conflict, status and subtext.
summary: Every line should convey attitude, a relationship shift or plot movement instead of empty social exchange.
details: Identify the conversation's objective, retain status differences, emotional pressure and hidden demands, then compress the rest.
pitfalls: Circular small talk and repeated explanations leave the situation unchanged.
positive_example: “Your conclusion.” He ignored the cup and watched her file. “I'll sign. First tell me why you went behind my back last night.”
negative_example: “You're here.” “Yes.” “How are you?” “Fine, and you?” Nothing advances.

intent_synonyms: how to write an argument|farewell scenes|advance emotional scenes
model_instruction: Use buildup, eruption and aftermath rather than beginning with mutual shouting.
summary: Accumulate conflict and pressure, cross a breaking point, then show the aftershock and changed relationship.
details: Establish positions during buildup, concentrate accusations and counterattacks at the peak, and close with silence, action or setting.
applicable_scenes: Heated disputes, farewells, uncontrolled confessions, failed apologies
pitfalls: An unprepared eruption or an argument with no lasting relational consequence.
positive_example: She laid the letter down quietly. Only when he said, “I never promised you,” did her fingers clench and the words she had held back all chapter pour out.
negative_example: They shout from the opening line, then the scene cuts away as though nothing changed.

intent_synonyms: how to stage combat|combat positioning|use terrain in fights
model_instruction: Establish beats and positioning, then integrate terrain, pauses and the finishing blow; do not stage combat in a vacuum.
summary: Attacks, dodges, counters, traps and environmental interactions need a readable rhythm.
details: Move from rapid exchanges to a pause to a decisive technique; broken cover and changes of distance should clarify the fight.
applicable_scenes: Tactical duels, group battles, final showdowns, competing abilities
pitfalls: Listing attacks and results without position, spatial relationships or environmental feedback.
positive_example: After driving his opponent back, he sidestepped into dust from the falling wall, leaving the concealed talisman spike exactly where the other man would land.
negative_example: They traded many fierce blows, then the protagonist used his strongest move and won.

intent_synonyms: how to plant clues|pay off foreshadowing|schedule long arcs
model_instruction: Separate core, subplot and decorative clues; assign payoff windows and fallback plans rather than endlessly planting new hints.
summary: Distinguish a clue's weight, introduction and payoff window so not every detail carries equal emphasis.
details: Core clues reverse the main plot, subplot clues add layers, and decorative clues add reality; give each a surface explanation and true meaning.
applicable_scenes: Mystery threads|long main arcs|identity reversals|world revelations
pitfalls: Over-obvious clues|unresolved setups|no intermediate reminders
positive_example: He dismissed the old key as junk. Thirty chapters later, it proved the only way into the sealed room.
negative_example: Scatter random strange details, then invent explanations for whichever ones become useful.

intent_synonyms: how to keep group dialogue clear|who is speaking|ensemble speech
model_instruction: Anchor each contribution in action, gaze or position so the speaking order and thought process remain traceable.
summary: Use action anchors, silent reactions and distinct syntax rather than a string of quotation marks.
details: With four or more people, interruptions, observations and silences must carry information or the scene blurs.
pitfalls: Everyone takes turns mechanically|silent characters disappear|speakers become indistinguishable
positive_example: He set his cup upside down. The man who had stayed silent in the corner suddenly looked toward the door.
negative_example: A speaks, then B, C and D, like a roll call.

keywords: scene cards|scene structure|goal conflict turn outcome|scene design
intent_synonyms: how to structure a scene|write scene cards|what a scene needs
model_instruction: Specify goal, conflict, turn and outcome before drafting to avoid elegant but purposeless scenes.
summary: Goal, conflict, turn and outcome form a reliable scene skeleton that forces meaningful progression.
details: The goal explains the scene's existence; conflict supplies tension, the turn changes it, and the outcome carries consequences forward.
pitfalls: Emotion without a goal|conflict without a turn|no downstream consequence
positive_example: He attended the banquet to test his enemies, but an assassin forced him to choose sides early and expose his identity.
negative_example: A tavern conversation adds no information and changes neither relationships nor circumstances.

intent_synonyms: how to use special powers|avoid cost-free cheats|make costs real
model_instruction: Connect desperation, activation, effect, immediate cost and aftermath; power cannot provide gratification without consequences.
summary: A special ability should deliver both reversal and cost, becoming a turning point rather than a free solution button.
details: First prove ordinary methods insufficient, then show the power and immediate weakness, exposure or relational consequences.
applicable_scenes: Desperate reversals|late-story trump cards|system bursts|forbidden techniques
pitfalls: No reason to use the power|cost delayed indefinitely|instant recovery
positive_example: The black blade split the blockade. A moment later his knees struck the ground, his wrist burning as though the bone were cracking from within.
negative_example: Whenever danger appears, he uses a cheat and suffers no physical or strategic consequences.

intent_synonyms: how to plant red herrings|build a false suspect|fair misdirection
model_instruction: Give false clues reasonable independent explanations that survive the reveal; do not simply deceive through authorial fiat.
summary: Fair misdirection makes readers recognize biased information on rereading rather than feel cheated.
details: Give the obvious suspect a real secret unrelated to the crime, allowing suspicious behavior to obscure a quieter culprit.
pitfalls: Unexplained false clues|a culprit introduced at the end|equally obvious suspects
positive_example: The maid fled because she had broken a vase, not stolen the diamond, but her panic drew every eye.
negative_example: Repeatedly imply one person is guilty, then admit it was only a trick without reconciling the evidence.

intent_synonyms: how to design a scheme|small acts cause big results|plot a chain reaction
model_instruction: Make the opening move appear unrelated to the outcome while ensuring every causal step can be reconstructed.
summary: The pleasure of an intricate scheme lies in discovering how every small disturbance was prepared.
details: Design the outcome first, then reverse-engineer how buying flowers, swapping seats or opening windows produces it.
pitfalls: Broken causal links|opening move too directly reveals outcome|reveal still makes no sense
positive_example: He bought flowers that triggered an allergy; the maid opened a window, drawing the guard away from the candle and exposing the assassin's line of sight.
negative_example: The protagonist performs many apparently clever errands, none necessary to the eventual result.

keywords: game theory|battle of wits|psychological strategy|anticipation and counterplay
intent_synonyms: how to write smart conflict|psychological warfare|three-round strategy
model_instruction: Explain the rules, then escalate cooperation, betrayal and counterplay; hidden information alone is not intelligence.
summary: Readers need rules, incentives and predictions to see victory as reasoning rather than favoritism.
details: Raise the stakes over two or three rounds: initial cooperation sets up betrayal and a final counter.
pitfalls: Unclear rules|victory through unexplained knowledge|opponents never adapt
positive_example: He surrendered a small advantage in round one to expose his opponent's greed; the real trap depended on the settlement timing in round three.
negative_example: They exchange threats, then a sudden bright idea wins the contest.

intent_synonyms: hide a clue in ordinary detail|foreshadow without giving it away
model_instruction: Disguise clues as incidental objects, slips of the tongue or setting details, with a planned later echo.
summary: An apparently casual remark, object or repeated gesture can become meaningful at payoff.
details: Embed clues naturally in dialogue and habits, knowing how they will return, rather than conspicuously winking at the reader.
pitfalls: Obvious signposting|no payoff|a reveal unsupported by earlier text
positive_example: He always touched his left ring finger when nervous. Only when the ring's secret emerged did readers understand.
negative_example: Describe an ordinary cup in bold ten times, then insist later that it mattered.

intent_synonyms: synchronize weather and plot|make settings change|use light emotionally
model_instruction: Describe change rather than static labels; let weather and light develop with action and emotion.
summary: An effective environment moves with arguments, pursuit, fear and relief rather than serving as a backdrop.
details: Distant thunder becoming rain, dusk darkening, or steady candles flickering can advance tension without adding adjectives.
pitfalls: Opening description never changes|setting unrelated to emotion|empty atmosphere words
positive_example: Thunder began far away. By the time she said, “You never trusted me,” rain seemed ready to pound through the street.
negative_example: The opening says the sky is cloudy; afterward the weather remains frozen regardless of events.

intent_synonyms: how to write case files|SCP-style horror|frightening experiment records
model_instruction: Maintain clinical detachment; let disturbing facts, redactions and omissions create horror rather than inserting lyrical emotion.
summary: Calmly recording profoundly abnormal facts lets readers supply the fear themselves.
details: Identifiers, containment procedures, test logs, redactions and abruptly terminated records create pseudoscientific credibility and dread.
pitfalls: Emotional exclamations|explaining everything|inconsistent format like a casual essay
positive_example: Appendix IV: Subject D-9341 disappeared three seconds after eating toasted bread. Residue recovered: 0.3 grams of crumbs.
negative_example: The anomaly was terrifying and everyone was frightened; the scene was incredibly dramatic.

intent_synonyms: how to use slang|jargon without confusion|regional dialogue
model_instruction: Use slang sparingly for key terms and make meaning inferable from context; avoid a wall of terminology.
summary: A few insider expressions establish profession and place more effectively than relentless jargon.
details: Replace frequent terms such as police, money, accomplices or enemies, then establish meaning through a natural example or two.
applicable_scenes: Gang negotiations|black markets|street criminals|internal organization talk
pitfalls: A dozen unexplained terms in one paragraph|no contextual support|everyone uses identical slang
positive_example: “The blues swept two streets. Keep the shine tucked away tonight.” The newcomer hurried to hide his coins and nodded.
negative_example: Every line is full of unfamiliar words with no context to explain them.

keywords: supporting-character side stories|missing motivation|alternate viewpoint|bonus chapters
intent_synonyms: how to write character extras|deepen supporting characters|side-story design
model_instruction: Fill motivational gaps rather than replaying the main story; explain the supporting character's decisive choices.
summary: A useful side story reveals hidden motives and actions instead of merely offering comfort or suffering to fans.
details: Choose an earlier period, a parallel timeline or the unseen side of an event to reinterpret a silence or betrayal.
applicable_scenes: Popular character spinoffs|main-story gaps|hidden actions revealed
pitfalls: Repeating existing scenes|abrupt personality changes|fan service without new information
positive_example: In the main story he simply handed over a key. The side story reveals the three years he spent infiltrating the enemy camp to steal it.
negative_example: Retell an unchanged main-story scene from someone else's mouth without adding value.

intent_synonyms: how to explain a fight|use a referee|show why a move is strong
model_instruction: Explain only decisive tactics and costs; do not narrate the duel like an instruction manual.
summary: Limited commentary in public competitions can clarify strategy and amplify the satisfaction of clever moves.
details: Explain why a move counters another, why an error matters and what may happen next instead of repeating actions.
applicable_scenes: Academy contests|public arenas|professional competition|complex ability duels
pitfalls: Repeating visible actions|constant interruptions|surprise without judgment
positive_example: “The ice mirror isn't reflecting the fireball,” the referee said. “He's baiting his opponent into wasting another twenty percent of his mana.”
negative_example: The commentator only shouts how fast and impressive everything is.

intent_synonyms: how to define chapter tasks|chapter planning|chapter purpose
model_instruction: Give each chapter plot, character, information and emotion tasks, not merely an event list.
summary: Useful chapter outlines specify four kinds of work alongside the sequence of events.
details: This reveals chapters that advance events but not characters, or express emotion without changing knowledge, reducing filler at the planning stage.
pitfalls: Only events listed|no character or information change|emotion left entirely to improvisation
positive_example: Catch the informant; make the hero first doubt his mentor; reveal the key's use; offer a partial payoff after pressure.
negative_example: Go to the market, fight, go home. Nothing else is defined.

keywords: paragraph outline|five to ten blocks|paragraph function|chapter segmentation
intent_synonyms: how to divide a chapter|paragraph planning|internal structure
model_instruction: Divide a chapter into five to ten functional blocks with one main objective each, then plan transitions and hooks.
summary: Functional blocks turn a vague chapter into executable units and reduce mid-draft confusion.
details: Break opening, setup, turn, climax and closure into smaller units, each with a clear advance and approximate length.
pitfalls: Overlapping functions|excessive fragmentation|no block-ending hooks
positive_example: Block one establishes setting and goal; two plants an anomaly; three erupts into conflict; four reverses it; five delivers the ending hook.
negative_example: One long chapter summary leaves the writer unsure what any individual section must do.

keywords: writing input packet|pre-draft synthesis|chapter materials|writing overview
intent_synonyms: how to assemble a writing packet|organize references before drafting
model_instruction: Collect tasks, scenes, key lines, character states and constraints into one readable overview instead of consulting ten documents while writing.
summary: A chapter input packet reduces forgotten details and drift by centralizing frequently needed information.
details: Include chapter tasks, scene sequence, key-line positions, current character states, prohibited setting changes and supplemental material summaries.
applicable_scenes: Pre-draft preparation|multi-document collaboration|continuous long-form work|continuity protection
pitfalls: An oversized document graveyard|no priorities|still requiring fresh extraction from sources
positive_example: One page records the plot task, hook, character states and setting limits, minimizing document hopping.
negative_example: References are scattered across folders; improvised browsing repeatedly creates continuity errors.

intent_synonyms: how to avoid duplicate characters|assign supporting functions
model_instruction: Give every supporting character an irreplaceable function and a memorable trait, not merely a different name.
summary: Clear functions help supporting characters remain relevant because readers understand what would be missing without them.
details: Information, emotion, combat and ideological mirrors are useful roles; avoid overcrowding any one function.
applicable_scenes: Cast planning|ensemble expansion|removing redundant characters|long-term cast maintenance
pitfalls: Interchangeable names|frequent appearances without purpose|overlapping functions
positive_example: The strategist interprets intelligence, the junior disciple carries emotional tension, and the old servant remembers the past. Each is necessary.
negative_example: Several friends do nothing but flatter the hero and express surprise.

intent_synonyms: how to link chapters|smooth chapter transitions
model_instruction: At each ending, identify the conflict carried forward and the new thread planted; continuity and preparation must coexist.
summary: Good transitions continue an old problem while quietly introducing the next arc's fuse.
details: Identify the inherited issue, the present change and the future setup: what remains, what shifts, and what will matter next.
pitfalls: Resolving without preparing|abrupt location shifts break emotion|time jumps explained only by narration
positive_example: After obtaining the secret letter, the next chapter deals with pursuers and uses a marginal note to open the capital-city arc.
negative_example: A life-or-death battle is followed by casual dining as if the conflict never happened.

keywords: payoff pressure hook|chapter balance|reward tension hook|chapter design
intent_synonyms: how to make a chapter gripping|balance chapter contents
model_instruction: Include a small payoff, a rise in pressure and an ending hook so readers receive a reward and want to continue.
summary: Serialized chapters sustain engagement through a combination of satisfaction, pressure and forward pull.
details: The payoff rewards, pressure stores energy and the hook extends interest; omitting any element can make a chapter feel flat.
technique_name: One payoff, one pressure rise, one hook
pitfalls: Explanation without reward|unrelieved pressure|a flat full-stop ending
positive_example: A clever move wins a small victory, reveals a larger enemy scheme, then a third party arrives at the door.
negative_example: The chapter explains the setting without a win, urgency or an enticing ending.

intent_synonyms: how to track clues|number foreshadowing|remember long arcs
model_instruction: Assign important clues IDs, planting chapters and expected payoff windows; do not rely on memory.
summary: A ledger makes foreshadowing traceable across volumes rather than an intuition exercise.
details: Useful fields include ID, planting location, type, importance, expected payoff chapter and fallback revision plan.
pitfalls: Unrecorded clues|forgotten original form|important clues buried in noise
positive_example: F-017: key notch planted in chapter 12; door-opening payoff in chapter 48; high importance.
negative_example: A casually mentioned pendant suddenly becomes the main key late in the story, but no earlier setup can be found.

keywords: five scene elements|information imagery conflict emotion hook|scene analysis
intent_synonyms: how to break down a scene|what a scene requires
model_instruction: Specify information, imagery, conflict, emotion and hook for each scene; rebuild scenes missing essential functions.
summary: The five elements expose circular scenes and identify why the reading experience fails.
details: Information advances understanding, imagery makes it visible, conflict drives action, emotion creates involvement and hooks encourage continuation.
pitfalls: Information without imagery|atmosphere without conflict|no onward pull
positive_example: A teahouse meeting reveals the letter, establishes the crowd and cups, brings a pursuer closer, and ends on a mismatched password.
negative_example: Two people explain lore for half a chapter with no image, risk or consequence.

keywords: planned key lines|opening line|turning-point line|climax line|closing line
intent_synonyms: how to plan memorable lines|opening sentences|chapter-end cuts
model_instruction: Plan key opening, turning-point, climax and closing lines so the chapter has anchors at its strongest moments.
summary: Planning key lines establishes four points of emphasis without dictating every sentence.
details: Work backward from the lines to setup and transitions, increasing memorable moments throughout the chapter.
applicable_scenes: Opening chapters|climax chapters|heavy emotional scenes|ending hooks
pitfalls: No memorable sentence|bad timing|striking words without preparation
positive_example: Open with an anomalous judgment, reserve a middle reversal, deliver the climax's verdict, then end with a new question.
negative_example: Add a quotable line after finishing the chapter, only to find it disconnected from the surrounding emotion.

intent_synonyms: how to pace chapter emotions|avoid flat paragraphs
model_instruction: Map emotional highs and lows before drafting, then decide where to accelerate and ease off.
summary: A paragraph-level curve prevents monotony and exposes climaxes that arrive too early or scatter their force.
details: A useful pattern is introduction, rise, imbalance, eruption and aftermath, with steepness adjusted to genre.
applicable_scenes: Action chapters|emotional chapters|mystery chapters|strong serialized units
pitfalls: Constant intensity causes fatigue|early climax leaves a long tail|no breathing space
positive_example: Begin with restrained probing, lose control midway, collide at the climax, then allow a brief silence before the hook.
negative_example: Shouting from the first paragraph to the last produces noise without a peak.

intent_synonyms: how to write a recap|summarize the previous volume
model_instruction: Extract turning points, character changes and unresolved questions; a recap should be concentrated story, not a chronological inventory.
summary: A good recap reconnects returning readers emotionally and tells newcomers what truly changed.
details: Select three to five major events, protagonist changes and world revelations; discard minor details.
pitfalls: Listing every incident|facts without emotion|omitting essential changes to avoid spoilers
positive_example: Begin with the breakthrough and loss, show the protagonist's changed standing, then identify the unresolved major question.
negative_example: A chronological account of every errand makes readers skip the recap halfway through.

intent_synonyms: how to tease the next volume|end-volume anticipation
model_instruction: Name challenges, people and direction without revealing solutions; anticipation should arise from what remains unsaid.
summary: Tell readers a larger storm is coming without explaining which door it will enter through.
details: Tease a new location, enemy or reopened mystery while leaving answers to the story.
applicable_scenes: Volume endings|after event chapters|before major transitions
pitfalls: A full plot synopsis|empty promises of excitement|spoiling the mystery
positive_example: The gates of the capital finally opened. What waited beyond them was not the reinforcement he expected.
negative_example: Next volume he visits the emperor, identifies the culprit and rescues his mentor.

intent_synonyms: how to write rules|handbook format|realistic instructions
model_instruction: Make the format convincing first, then introduce small anomalies; horror comes from abnormal instructions in an ordinary wrapper.
summary: A rules document is most unsettling when it looks entirely routine.
details: Numbers, clauses, advisory language and cautions create an official appearance that makes anomalous content stand out.
applicable_scenes: Scenario entry|secret organization manuals|school rules|horror notices
pitfalls: Supernatural claims everywhere|loose essay format|too many anomalies to establish normality
positive_example: Turn off the lights before nine. If someone in the corridor counts to four, do not open your door.
negative_example: These rules are terrifying. Do not die or the monster will come.

keywords: contradictory rules|parallel clues|true and false instructions|reader deduction
intent_synonyms: how to introduce conflicting rules|enable reader inference
model_instruction: Present conflicting rules together but make at least one verifiable through evidence; confusion must not rest on arbitrary cheating.
summary: Contradictions should force characters and readers to judge which instruction preserves life, not merely bewilder them.
details: Direct, temporal or identity-based contradictions need environmental evidence or character reactions for verification.
pitfalls: Random contradictions|no verifying clues|the author simply announces the answer
positive_example: The handbook calls the red door safe, but the attendant desperately blocks anyone approaching it.
negative_example: Two rules contradict each other and the text offers nothing from which to reason.

intent_synonyms: how to hide rules|setting evidence|behavior reveals constraints
model_instruction: Distribute hidden-rule evidence across setting, objects and people so the reveal is reconstructable rather than a lucky insight.
summary: Rules should already be present in arrangements, unusual objects and habits before their meaning emerges.
details: Setting supplies repeated anomalies, objects supply tangible evidence and people supply behavioral deviations; combine all three.
pitfalls: All clues in dialogue|decorative settings|no earlier basis for the reveal
positive_example: Dust always lacks one corner by the window, a handbook page is missing, and the guard steps back whenever the fourth floor is mentioned.
negative_example: At the reveal, announce an extra hidden rule with no previous sign of it.

keywords: deduction chain|hypothesis evidence elimination|logical closure|truth reveal
intent_synonyms: how to show deduction|build a logical chain|derive the truth step by step
model_instruction: Proceed through observation, hypothesis, evidence, elimination and conclusion so readers can reconstruct the reasoning.
summary: Every deduction needs premises, evidence and alternatives, not merely a declaration of understanding.
details: Even a startling conclusion should feel retrospectively inevitable rather than like an improvised authorial turn.
pitfalls: Sudden omniscience|large gaps between evidence and conclusion|unsupported elimination
positive_example: Confirm two rules conflict, use prior deaths to eliminate the false rule, then identify the hidden premise that leaves one safe route.
negative_example: Without evidence, the protagonist suddenly declares the director the mastermind.

keywords: show don't tell|embodied emotion|indirect emotion|emotional action
intent_synonyms: how to show anger|show fear through action|avoid emotion labels
model_instruction: Prefer actions, microexpressions and environmental feedback to abstract emotional labels.
summary: Replace “he was angry” with a concrete response readers can see, hear or feel.
details: White knuckles, a difficult swallow or an interrupted sentence create immediacy more effectively than labels.
pitfalls: Too many actions obscure focus|every feeling becomes clenched fists|setting and reaction disconnected
positive_example: She never said she was afraid. By her third check of the lock, her fingertips had gone pale and cold.
negative_example: She was frightened, very frightened, entirely filled with fear.

intent_synonyms: how to write original metaphors|avoid cliched comparisons
model_instruction: Match metaphors to the book's tone; use unfamiliar but understandable images instead of worn comparisons.
summary: A fresh metaphor can deepen emotion and world atmosphere at once, not merely decorate a sentence.
details: Wounds, mildew and old bones may suit horror; exaggeration and incongruity may suit light comedy. Do not mix registers carelessly.
pitfalls: Incomprehensible novelty|images alien to the viewpoint|constant verbal showmanship
positive_example: His smile was thin ice lodged between bones: bright, and ready to crack underfoot.
negative_example: She was beautiful as a flower and sad as rain, adding no fresh perception.

intent_synonyms: how to create immersive settings|combine senses
model_instruction: Use two or three senses and connect them to the character's emotion or immediate task pressure.
summary: Sensory layers turn setting into something that physically bears on a character.
details: Neon reflected in water, rain on tin, refuse odors and blood in the mouth can combine into a convincing lived scene.
pitfalls: Only visual detail|all senses given equal weight|setting detached from the character
positive_example: Rain rattled the tin roof as sewer rot rose through the alley, making it feel like an old pot beginning to steam.
negative_example: The alley was dark and damp. Nothing further makes it tangible.

intent_synonyms: how to unite storylines|keep an ensemble coherent
model_instruction: Draw subplots toward a volume-scale event instead of letting interesting characters remain permanently separate.
summary: Multiple narratives gain strength when they meet at a point that changes one another's destinies.
details: A siege, final battle, explosion at a festival or disaster can activate the value of dispersed characters at once.
pitfalls: Unrelated subplots|a weak meeting instead of convergence|frequent viewpoint cuts without payoff
positive_example: The military, court and civilian storylines collided on the night the capital was besieged.
negative_example: Every character has a story, but at the end they still seem to belong to different books.

intent_synonyms: how characters change|design a growth catalyst
model_instruction: Force change through a concrete event rather than having a character suddenly understand everything.
summary: An arc is not a new label; an event must bring old wounds, old choices and new costs into collision.
details: A mentor's death, betrayal, failed mission or injured child can break a character out of an old way of thinking.
pitfalls: Personality changes without cause|instant transformation|later behavior unchanged
positive_example: He did not suddenly become responsible. After burying his mentor himself, he began making decisions for others.
negative_example: A selfish, cold character becomes indiscriminately compassionate between chapters with no trigger.

intent_synonyms: how to write unreliable narrators|plant subtle inconsistencies
model_instruction: Make the account plausible first, then introduce discrepancies in time, physical detail or memory without exposing the answer immediately.
summary: Readers should sense something wrong before they can name it.
details: Omitted blood, displaced chronology or others never responding to a supposed companion can support a fair later reveal.
pitfalls: Obvious discrepancies|pure concealment of crucial facts|reveal cannot reconcile earlier scenes
positive_example: His account of the crime scene always avoids the mirror, the one object that would reveal the truth.
negative_example: Withhold half the facts and introduce them at the reveal to force a reversal.

intent_synonyms: how to connect two timelines|clear flashbacks|past and present parallels
model_instruction: Give both timelines a shared object or image; the past should explain the present rather than merely consume pages.
summary: A recurring anchor whose meaning changes provides a stronger connection than arbitrary viewpoint cuts.
details: A broken watch, old photograph, chipped key or unsent letter can translate between timelines.
pitfalls: Timelines feel unrelated|arbitrary switches|the past changes nothing about the present
positive_example: The present-day watch is stopped at 7:13; the past timeline eventually reveals why it can never move beyond that moment.
negative_example: Flashbacks merely add background and can be removed without affecting the present story.

intent_synonyms: how to make profiling credible|infer character from evidence
model_instruction: Tie every profiling conclusion to physical evidence or behavioral traces; analysis is inference, not divination.
summary: Evidence-based profiling gives character inference logic and gradually makes the culprit feel real.
details: Overkill, cleanup, souvenirs and repeated routes support a profile better than unsupported psychological claims.
pitfalls: Premature conclusions|mismatched evidence|genius intuition replacing reasoning
positive_example: She notes the clean windowsill before concluding the killer did not climb in at random but knew the house.
negative_example: One glance supposedly reveals an unloved childhood and the precise district of the next crime without supporting evidence.

intent_synonyms: how to check a payoff|make readers remember clues
model_instruction: Before the payoff, verify readers can recall the planted clues and that the reveal explains each earlier anomaly.
summary: A strong answer immediately recalls small irregularities readers previously overlooked.
details: Check that clues exist, are not too obvious, and correspond individually to the reveal.
pitfalls: Explosive reveal with weak setup|over-obvious hints|unexplained anomalies remain
positive_example: When the butler is exposed, his wiped door handles, absence and casual complaint all connect at once.
negative_example: Readers reread the story after the reveal and find no plausible supporting clue.

intent_synonyms: how weather moves with plot|use light to build atmosphere
model_instruction: Show weather changing in stages and synchronize those changes with emotion and conflict.
summary: Dynamic settings develop alongside relationships and circumstances instead of remaining static scenery.
details: Distant thunder, sudden rain, stopped wind, fading daylight or a break in clouds can mark emotional beats.
pitfalls: Decorative weather|unprepared abrupt changes|setting overwhelms characters
positive_example: She kept denying it while the rain outside thickened from lines into a white wall, pushing the atmosphere to breaking point.
negative_example: Clear skies become a thunderstorm in one sentence solely because the author wants drama.

intent_synonyms: how to use silent participants|undercurrents in meetings
model_instruction: Track silent participants' actions and gaze; they may reveal danger more effectively than the current speaker.
summary: Silence invites questions about what a character is withholding or observing.
details: Sweat, hesitation, pressed lips, glances at the door and avoided eye contact can carry clues and tension.
pitfalls: Silent people disappear|speech replaces all action|everyone talks and overloads the scene
positive_example: While everyone argued about the route, the man in the corner never looked up, but his paper cup split under his fingers.
negative_example: Four people speak for three pages while a fifth vanishes from the author's attention.

intent_synonyms: how to manage chronology|reverse-plan an outline|when to skip time
model_instruction: Work backward from the ending to key years and growth targets, then choose which periods to dramatize or skip.
summary: Time constraints should tighten structure rather than merely record events.
details: Fixing the demon's awakening in year ten, war in year three and enrollment in year one clarifies the overall pace.
applicable_scenes: Long outlines|multi-year history|growth and progression fiction
pitfalls: Ages contradict events|training fills every interval|unmarked time jumps
positive_example: If the frontier must be defended in three years, the protagonist cannot still be doing novice errands at the end of year one.
negative_example: Ten volumes depict a twenty-year-old protagonist while only three months pass.

intent_synonyms: how to order sensory detail|avoid sensory overload
model_instruction: Let one dominant sense lead and support it with two others rather than listing all five equally.
summary: The richer the sensory description, the more it needs hierarchy to remain clear.
details: Use sight to establish, sound to pressure and touch to close, or start with touch and supplement through smell and sound.
pitfalls: Every sense at once|constant switching loses focus|adjectives without action
positive_example: Damp mildew reached her through the door first. Then footsteps sounded, each striking the hollow wooden floor.
negative_example: The room is dark, cold, quiet, foul and damp: a list of every available sensation.

intent_synonyms: how to connect small actions|sequence microexpressions
model_instruction: Break an emotional beat into three or four visible connected actions instead of jumping straight to collapse.
summary: Linked microactions make emotion and relationships observable processes.
details: Shifting eyes, pausing fingers, changing breath, tensing shoulders and unfinished words can form a sequence.
pitfalls: Only an end result|emotion and action disconnected|repeated lip-biting and fist-clenching
positive_example: She reached for the cup, stopped at its rim, then pushed it toward him without looking up.
negative_example: She bites her lip, clenches her fists, trembles and cries all at once, without progression.

intent_synonyms: how to write subtext|dialogue undercurrents|concealed intentions
model_instruction: Define both the surface and hidden objective of a conversation, maintaining tension between words and desired outcomes.
summary: Subtext means visible conversation and underlying strategy happen together, not merely vague speech.
details: A greeting can probe, a joke can interrogate and thanks can establish a boundary; connect each line to a real objective.
pitfalls: Meaning wholly left to guesses|lines unrelated to goals|endless evasions without information
positive_example: He asks whether she is sleeping well, really checking whether she still takes the medication that makes her hands shake.
negative_example: Everyone speaks in riddles and communicates nothing, leaving only confusion.

intent_synonyms: how to hook the first paragraph|result-first opening
model_instruction: Open with an abnormal outcome or high-pressure present, then supply necessary causes by the shortest route.
summary: Front-loading is about showing that something is wrong now, not rushing through lore.
details: A canceled wedding, a missing corpse or a new name in the rules creates immediate interest; add only essential background.
pitfalls: Necessary context delayed too long|opening history lesson|hook unrelated to main plot
positive_example: Ten minutes before the wedding, a photograph arrived. Beside the groom stood me, buried three years earlier.
negative_example: Long ago there was a world; first, let us explain its history and systems.

intent_synonyms: how to accelerate narration|clear scene cuts
model_instruction: Every cut must add information, pressure or a goal rather than change scenery without purpose.
summary: Fast prose advances the situation in every paragraph; short sentences alone do not suffice.
details: Alternate action, reaction, evidence and countdown beats to maintain density and direction.
pitfalls: Fragments without causality|disorienting speed|repeated information
positive_example: The elevator fell, her phone vibrated, police lights flashed below, and the voice message she had sent finally showed delivered.
negative_example: Scenes keep switching but reveal nothing new, producing only confusion.

keywords: rule contradictions|cross-checking|true and false rules|hidden rules
intent_synonyms: how to audit rules horror|find hidden conditions
model_instruction: Compare rules by subject, time, space and exceptions to identify statements that cannot both be true.
summary: Rule-based stories gain interest when characters and readers discover where instructions fail to align.
details: A ban on leaving after lights-out conflicts with midnight meal collection; a condition table makes that conflict usable.
pitfalls: Rules are merely scary sentences|contradictions never tested|new rules announced arbitrarily
positive_example: Reordering rules by time reveals the cafeteria is forbidden only to people without staff badges.
negative_example: Contradictions are ignored until the author arbitrarily chooses which rule applies.

intent_synonyms: how to write rigorous deduction|structure rule inference
model_instruction: Propose several possibilities, then eliminate them through evidence instead of jumping to the official answer.
summary: Readers enjoy watching plausible wrong hypotheses fall to successive evidence.
details: Use chronology, testimony, traces and rule constraints to narrow possibilities rather than rely on inspiration.
pitfalls: Sudden revelation|evidence supports only the answer|no plausible wrong branches
positive_example: They suspect the administrator changed the roster, but footage proves he never went upstairs; suspicion returns to the newcomer claiming not to know the rules.
negative_example: The protagonist glances at the scene, says “I understand,” and announces the truth.

intent_synonyms: how to seed alternate endings|prepare true-ending requirements
model_instruction: Plant each ending's choices, costs and clues early so divergence feels like resolution rather than a new story.
summary: The number of endings matters less than whether each follows real earlier choices.
details: Safety can lead to an ordinary ending while exploration and greater cost unlock the true one; establish conditions in advance.
applicable_scenes: Long-story endings|scenario true endings|alternate-universe extras|repeated-run structures
pitfalls: Last-minute secret conditions|cosmetic variants|choices unrelated to outcomes
positive_example: Twice in volume two he refuses to destroy the old ticket. Only at the end does it become the final pass to the true outcome.
negative_example: A hidden task appears one chapter before the ending and is declared the perfect-ending requirement.

intent_synonyms: how to release evidence|layer an investigation
model_instruction: First supply directional evidence, then contradictory evidence, reserving the decisive proof rather than revealing everything at once.
summary: Evidence order makes investigation readable and allows the truth to pull readers forward.
details: Move from observed phenomena to contradictions to decisive proof so readers revise their judgments alongside the characters.
pitfalls: Decisive proof too early|confusing order|all evidence recited together
positive_example: They establish the victim left the ward, uncover a camera blind spot, and only then place the swapped slippers on the table.
negative_example: The protagonist opens with conclusive evidence, rendering all subsequent analysis pointless.

keywords: misdirection and truth|parallel clues|fair reversals|dual setup
intent_synonyms: how to mislead fairly|plant true and false trails
model_instruction: Make the misleading trail coherent but incomplete and the true trail present but unobtrusive; both must develop together.
summary: A strong twist offers a convincing wrong route alongside the genuine clues.
details: Behavior, speech, rules and chronology can mislead, while exceptions and anomalies quietly expose the real route.
pitfalls: Obviously false decoys|invisible true clues|earlier events cannot be reconciled
positive_example: Everyone watches the talkative nurse, overlooking the cleaner who switches off the lights thirty seconds early at every handover.
negative_example: The author hides decisive information instead of preparing the reversal.

intent_synonyms: how to switch storylines clearly|transition anchors
model_instruction: Leave an unfinished action, object or question before switching, then orient the reader clearly at the new opening.
summary: Frequent switches require anchors showing where one thread stopped and another begins.
details: Time markers, character goals, objects and unfinished actions hold multiple threads together.
applicable_scenes: Ensemble novels|scenario and reality threads|parallel investigations|pre-battle separation
pitfalls: Suspense at the expense of clarity|no new-scene coordinates|unclear actors and actions
positive_example: He clenches the rusty key; the next chapter cuts to the docks three hours earlier, where the same key hangs at another man's waist.
negative_example: A hospital scene jumps to a basement without identifying time, place or participants.

intent_synonyms: how to structure intense emotion|pace an argument
model_instruction: Establish suppression, then a breaking point, then aftermath rather than beginning at maximum volume.
summary: Intensity comes from the continuity of buildup, eruption and resonance, not shouting alone.
details: Buildup establishes conflict, eruption exposes the deepest wound, and aftermath changes the relationship.
pitfalls: Maximum intensity immediately|instant reset after eruption|speech without aftermath
positive_example: She keeps saying she is fine. Only when he produces the old ticket stub does she truly look at him.
negative_example: They meet and collapse into tears after three lines, with no pressure or trigger established.

keywords: payoff pause|aftermath reactions|silent resonance|hold a beat
intent_synonyms: how to pause after a payoff|reactions after a counterattack
model_instruction: After a major payoff, allow a brief reaction beat before escalating again; continuous intensity flattens impact.
summary: A pause lets the event's weight land for both readers and witnesses rather than merely cooling the scene.
details: Silence, glances, dropped objects, altered forms of address and delayed applause deepen the preceding moment.
pitfalls: Immediate nonstop escalation|generic shocked reactions|pauses long enough to lose momentum
positive_example: For a second even the livestream comments seemed frozen. The first person to retrieve the microphone was the reporter who had shouted loudest.
negative_example: After winning, the hero lectures for three pages without allowing anyone to react.

keywords: immediate cost|ability side effects|instant consequences|power price
intent_synonyms: how to show power costs immediately|avoid free abilities
model_instruction: When a major ability activates, immediately show a physical, relational or world-level cost rather than postponing every consequence.
summary: Power becomes credible when its use visibly demands payment, not merely when narration promises one.
details: Blood, lost speech, missing memories, higher beings' attention, frightened allies or deepening contamination can provide immediate consequences.
pitfalls: No immediate effect despite promised costs|a later passing mention of fatigue|universal solution powers
positive_example: As he forced the door open, black marks climbed his veins and a teammate instinctively stepped away for the first time.
negative_example: Every power use is painless; only the author's warning claims otherwise.

intent_synonyms: how to make rules memorable|write convincing rules
model_instruction: Write short, precise, executable clauses that someone could genuinely follow, then introduce localized anomalies.
summary: Rules should first suggest a way to survive, with unease emerging from details rather than a pile of scary sentences.
details: Separate action, time, location and exception clauses; clarity supports later deduction and reversal.
pitfalls: Horror poetry instead of instructions|abstract prohibitions|unmemorable hidden anomalies
positive_example: After 23:00, do not enter the east corridor alone. If passage is unavoidable, switch off your flashlight and remain silent.
negative_example: If something feels wrong, do not trust them or face the consequences: atmospheric copy without usable instructions.

intent_synonyms: how to write an epilogue|leave an aftertaste
model_instruction: Return only to what deserves to remain, grounding closure in characters and motifs rather than opening a new conflict.
summary: An epilogue supplies an emotional landing and shows whom the story changed.
details: A letter, homecoming, revisited place or new habit can resonate more than a long account of the next ten years.
pitfalls: Opening new mysteries|life-history resumes|sweetness that ignores previous costs
positive_example: He finally learned to leave a little cilantro in his noodles. The old shop's light, for once, was not burning while someone waited.
negative_example: Twenty pages of new lore and another crisis dissolve the sense of closure.

intent_synonyms: how to plant natural clues|make payoffs convincing
model_instruction: Provide a reasonable surface explanation at first appearance, revealing the true meaning only at payoff.
summary: Natural foreshadowing gives a significant detail an ordinary explanation that is valid at the time.
details: Dialogue, objects, behavior and setting can all carry clues, provided the later interpretation feels earned rather than patched in.
pitfalls: Overemphasis on introduction|incompatible later meaning|unrecorded setup
positive_example: Nobody notices her sewing the old button back onto her sleeve until the missing person's uniform is found to use that exact kind.
negative_example: A mysterious object appears with no ordinary purpose, obviously waiting for a payoff.

intent_synonyms: how to show reasoning|make explanations engaging
model_instruction: Move through observation, hypothesis, evidence, counterevidence and conclusion so readers reason rather than merely receive an answer.
summary: Good deduction lets evidence progressively squeeze out wrong answers.
details: Tie every important conclusion to evidence and at least one eliminated hypothesis to maintain fairness.
pitfalls: Conclusions without evidence|last-minute clues|missing reasoning steps
positive_example: If the key was taken after ten, the footsteps at nine-thirty were not the killer's; someone prepared a false trail.
negative_example: The protagonist closes his eyes and knows the truth without connecting any clues.

intent_synonyms: how to evoke a period|avoid lists of old objects
model_instruction: Let institutions, supplies, forms of address and everyday actions affect the plot rather than treating historical objects as decoration.
summary: Period detail becomes story pressure only when it affects choices.
details: Ration coupons, work units, neighbors, cooperatives, food allowances and policy limits can enter action and dialogue naturally.
applicable_scenes: Period daily life|courtyard neighborhoods|workplace conflicts|family meals
pitfalls: Object catalogs|modern speech intrusions|historical limits never constrain choices
positive_example: She rolls her worn cuffs inward without mentioning a shortage of cloth. The older neighbor immediately understands why she refuses the matchmaker.
negative_example: An enamel mug and old radio decorate a room where everyone speaks modern corporate jargon.

intent_synonyms: how to write painful romance|make emotion concrete
model_instruction: Connect trigger, bodily reaction, action choice and interpretation rather than stacking words for suffering.
summary: Show why the character hurts and what she chooses afterward.
details: Sight, sound, touch, pauses and small gestures should connect to relationships or old wounds.
pitfalls: Abstract despair repeated|emotion unrelated to experience|tears change no action
positive_example: Hearing “just like her,” she does not cry. She slowly crosses out her signature until the pen tears the paper.
negative_example: She is terribly hurt, desperate and sad, filled with indescribably complex feelings.

intent_synonyms: how to write enemy plans|credible villain defeat
model_instruction: Show only what the antagonist knows and can reasonably infer, keeping the protagonist's true variable hidden.
summary: An antagonist's viewpoint should make the reader acknowledge the logic of the plan at the time.
details: Give resources, reasons and blind spots; let a previously planted small variable exploit the blind spot later.
pitfalls: Ignoring obvious clues|revealing too many protagonist secrets|sudden stupidity
positive_example: He researched every contestant but omitted the water carrier, who had still been unable to speak three months earlier.
negative_example: The villain sees all the evidence but refuses it solely because the author needs him to lose.

intent_synonyms: how to write believable first person|natural internal narration
model_instruction: Limit first person to perception and inference, using mistakes and blind spots rather than intrusive omniscience.
summary: First person's strengths are immediacy and uncertainty, not exhaustive explanation.
details: Keep inner speech close to present sensation, judgment and fear; minimize long lore lectures.
pitfalls: Knowing others' private thoughts|manual-like monologues|constant exposition
positive_example: The lock clicked twice. My first thought was not fear, but that I had flushed the spare key down the toilet last night.
negative_example: I know everyone's true thoughts and that the mastermind is hiding on the third floor.

intent_synonyms: how to make rules frightening|write concrete handbooks
model_instruction: Begin with executable clauses, then use detached wording and anomalous exceptions to create unease.
summary: The horror comes from treating absurd danger as an ordinary administrative requirement.
details: Short numbered statements, conditions, exceptions and unexplained consequences create realism and deductive value.
applicable_scenes: Rule notices|scenario manuals|hospital or school regulations|staff handbooks
pitfalls: Unusable poetic language|pure scare lines|no conditions or consequences
positive_example: After 23:00, do not respond to anyone calling your name in the corridor, including relatives.
negative_example: When night swallows the soul, listen to destiny's lament: mood copy, not a rule.

intent_synonyms: how to build dread|horror without jump scares
model_instruction: Progress from normality to small irregularities to the inexplicable rather than relying on sudden faces.
summary: Familiar everyday spaces make tiny deviations particularly unsettling.
details: Establish order, alter one sound, shadow, smell or spatial detail, then let the character realize a rule is approaching.
pitfalls: Immediate gore|no escalation|characters fail to react reasonably
positive_example: The corridor light flashed every three seconds. On the seventh flash, someone stood beneath it.
negative_example: A ghost face jumps out, then has no relation to the story's rules.

intent_synonyms: how to make fights clear|maintain combat geography
model_instruction: Keep positions, actions, reactions and results traceable instead of fragmenting the scene.
summary: Clear action depends on visible causality, not sheer quantity of detail.
details: Establish distance and stance before attacks, evasions, counters and costs; use environmental landmarks when needed.
pitfalls: Only visual effects and technique names|inconsistent distances|attacks without results
positive_example: Pinned left of the pillar with half a step of retreat, he strikes the pillar's base rather than his opponent.
negative_example: They become blurs for three hundred exchanges and nobody knows where either stands.

intent_synonyms: how to write painful subtext|meaningful silence
model_instruction: Use unequal knowledge so surface speech also exposes concealment, probing or avoidance.
summary: Replacement-lover dialogue hurts when neither person states the whole truth but details already wound them.
details: Old nicknames, pauses, corrections, avoided names and abrupt topic changes carry efficient subtext.
pitfalls: Everything explained directly|uninformative silence|subtext has no identifiable meaning
positive_example: “Do you like this color?” she asks. He pauses. “Someone used to.” The past tense hurts more than a name.
negative_example: “You treat me as a replacement and that makes me sad.” Stating the subtext removes the tension.

intent_synonyms: how to write restrained family emotion|daily-life resonance
model_instruction: Let ordinary actions and omissions carry hurt so readers infer it themselves.
summary: Social realism loses credibility when shouting substitutes for actual daily pressure.
details: Money, meals, illness, housing, work and neighbors' opinions can evoke emotion faster than lyrical declarations.
pitfalls: Narration announces all feelings|social reality absent|characters lack material lives
positive_example: She does not mention missing dinner. She gives her father the last piece of meat and drinks another mouthful of cold soup.
negative_example: The author announces her pain and her family's lack of understanding instead of dramatizing either.

intent_synonyms: how to introduce a new world quickly|compress mission information
model_instruction: Assemble identity through immediate danger and fragments of information rather than long system briefings.
summary: Let readers understand the new identity while experiencing the crisis instead of memorizing lore first.
details: Forms of address, objects, bodily states, phone records, reactions and brief prompts can jointly establish the world.
pitfalls: System dumps all background|long historical introduction|no immediate pressure
positive_example: Before she recognizes her face in the mirror, someone calls through the door: “Young mistress, the master orders you to the ancestral hall to confess.”
negative_example: The system recites twenty years of the original occupant's life before the scene begins.

intent_synonyms: how to write historical institutions|court dialogue|grounded political intrigue
model_instruction: Make offices, ritual and risk constrain choices rather than serve as background decoration.
summary: Historical credibility comes from people living under their era's rules, not modern people in costumes.
details: Reports, lineage, military orders, registration, taxes and etiquette should change what characters can say or do.
pitfalls: Unrestricted modern assumptions|institutions only in notes|casual breaches of hierarchy
positive_example: He does not immediately object: saying it in court would punish his sponsoring teacher before it harmed his opponent.
negative_example: The protagonist interrupts court like a modern meeting and every official accepts his reasoning.

keywords: business detail|cost and return|craft process|daily texture
intent_synonyms: how to write grounded enterprise|avoid business montages
model_instruction: Show costs, steps, failure and customer feedback rather than instant bestsellers.
summary: Craft and everyday detail give pastoral business stories texture; profit must arise through a real process.
details: Preparation, trials, wastage, pricing, test sales and repeat business can each reveal ability and pressure.
pitfalls: Skipping production|no costs|every customer buys unquestioningly
positive_example: Half the first sauce batch scorches. Rather than waste it, she uses its toasted aroma to adjust the heat for the second batch.
negative_example: She casually makes snacks, everyone calls them miraculous, and money pours in.

intent_synonyms: how to write cultivation|make breakthroughs meaningful
model_instruction: Show changes in body, mind and understanding rather than merely circulating energy through a fixed number of cycles.
summary: Cultivation scenes matter when the character's understanding of the Way, self and desire changes.
details: Breath, channels, still or moving surroundings, resurfacing thoughts and one insight into principles can carry the breakthrough.
pitfalls: Only surging energy|no mental change|a numerical upgrade
positive_example: Listening to rain at the eaves, she realizes she has not cultivated freedom from feeling, but fear of feeling.
negative_example: He sits, circulates energy thirty-six times and levels up.

intent_synonyms: how to distinguish world-hopping arcs|change narrative voice
model_instruction: Change vocabulary, relationship pressures and pacing with each world, not just names.
summary: Freshness comes from different rules and social logic.
details: School arcs emphasize reputation and youth; historical worlds emphasize rank and ritual; apocalypses emphasize resources and survival. Adapt the prose accordingly.
pitfalls: Identical speech everywhere|differences limited to clothing|unchanged mission logic
positive_example: In the previous world she could call the police. Here she needs the matriarch's token merely to leave the house.
negative_example: Every world's characters speak in the same contemporary internet-fiction voice.

intent_synonyms: how to write esports|make game actions readable
model_instruction: Combine mechanics, communication, map information and commentary rather than simply declaring the player strong.
summary: Readers enjoy understanding why a player excels, not only hearing praise.
details: Cooldowns, vision, objectives, positioning and team calls make skill visible.
pitfalls: Only fast hands and shocked audiences|unclear tactical value|commentary replaces action
positive_example: “No vision at dragon.” He saves his dash for a second entry, waiting for the enemy support to spend its crowd control.
negative_example: His hands move quickly, he performs a combo, and everyone is amazed.

intent_synonyms: how to make technology credible|avoid omnipotent inventions
model_instruction: Specify function, limits, cost and failure modes instead of letting advanced technology solve everything.
summary: Technical boundaries create credibility more effectively than impressive terminology.
details: Energy, heat, latency, access, maintenance and ethical costs can all generate conflict.
pitfalls: Cost-free universal technology|irrelevant jargon|convenient arbitrary failures
positive_example: The artificial eye sees through walls, but strong magnetism creates half a second of static, enough for the assassin to enter its blind spot.
negative_example: He activates a high-tech device and every problem disappears.

intent_synonyms: how to write divine and demonic romance|use supernatural intimacy
model_instruction: Make supernatural rules participate in both closeness and obstacles rather than dressing ordinary romance in magical identities.
summary: The sweetness and pain arise when feeling collides with species or supernatural law.
details: Bloodline responses, contract backlash, unequal lifespans, clan taboos and power resonance can become emotional details.
pitfalls: Magic is decoration|conflicts identical to contemporary romance|bloodline powers rescue everything
positive_example: When he touches her wrist, the contract mark does not glow; an older oath seems to press it dim, inch by inch.
negative_example: One is divine and one demonic, but their problems are indistinguishable from ordinary dating.

intent_synonyms: how to avoid out-of-character writing|match source material
model_instruction: Preserve canonical values and speech rhythms before designing new events.
summary: Borrowing a name without the character's underlying logic produces hollow fanfiction.
details: Events may change, but boundaries, reaction speed, address habits and core relationships need a reason to change.
pitfalls: Names without personalities|entirely new voices|new lore overrides canon
positive_example: He asks the price before agreeing to rescue anyone, fitting someone who never trusts miracles.
negative_example: A normally restrained character suddenly shouts that love solves everything for no reason.

intent_synonyms: how to evoke historical daily life|natural period voices
model_instruction: Put objects, ration coupons, workplaces and neighbors into actions rather than displaying them like exhibits.
summary: Period fiction gains credibility through material pressure and tightly connected communities.
details: Food, clothing, job places, courtyard gossip and family allocation should shape decisions.
pitfalls: Catalogs of old objects|modern assumptions in costume|dates are the only historical cue
positive_example: She sets the enamel mug at the table's edge and asks not about money, but whether this month's grain coupons will last.
negative_example: He lectures the courtyard on modern management and every neighbor is instantly convinced.

intent_synonyms: how to write historical dialogue|official forms of address
model_instruction: Reflect status, address and risk rather than letting everyone argue as equals in a modern workplace.
summary: Historical voice depends less on archaic words than on who is permitted to say what.
details: The same remark carries different risks at a family banquet, hearing, military tent or court; identify the local hierarchy first.
pitfalls: Modern voices throughout|confused titles|subordinates freely berate superiors
positive_example: The deputy answers with lowered eyes, first saying “Your Honor,” then gently shifting responsibility to the old seal in the ledger.
negative_example: A junior clerk slams the table: “Stop pretending. Let's all be candid.”

intent_synonyms: how to pace settlement building|show business progress
model_instruction: Solve survival before expansion; give every project materials, labor, time and returns.
summary: Satisfaction comes from visible improvement to an identified shortage, not a declaration that construction is finished.
details: Develop water, storage, roads, tools and trade channels in stages, paying off each through changed daily life.
pitfalls: Skipping the process|unlimited resources|residents only applaud
positive_example: The first bricks pave the grain-drying yard rather than a grand gate. After rain, the harvest no longer rots in mud.
negative_example: One order creates ten workshops and instantly makes the territory wealthy.

intent_synonyms: how to resolve world-hopping missions|pay off the host's regrets
model_instruction: Resolve the task, the original person's regrets and the world's costs together; do not jump away after a public humiliation scene.
summary: Completion should rewrite the host's fate and release the reader's accumulated resentment.
details: Establish oppressive relationships and task boundaries at the opening, then end with assessment, aftermath or emotional residue.
pitfalls: Gratification without closure|original person reduced to a tool|meaningless task ratings
positive_example: Before the system announces success, she burns the apology letter, ten years late, as an offering to the original host's mother.
negative_example: After humiliating everyone, she jumps to the next world and the original person's family is never mentioned again.

keywords: tribulation pressure|exhausted trump cards|human interference|willpower breakthrough
intent_synonyms: how to write thrilling ascension|pace heavenly tribulations
model_instruction: Combine natural catastrophe, human threats and inner demons, exhausting defenses before the breakthrough.
summary: Spectacle needs a real price for attaining the Way, not merely abundant lightning.
details: Broken artifacts, old enemies, inner questioning and bodily endurance should escalate until advancement becomes a choice rather than a reward.
pitfalls: Empty spectacle|endless trump cards|no meaningful choice
positive_example: When the final bolt falls, he summons no sword; he closes his hand around the two broken halves of his life-bound jade.
negative_example: Lightning flashes, he shouts that his fate is his own, and immediately ascends.

intent_synonyms: how to write cultivation debates|avoid hollow preaching
model_instruction: Tie arguments to cultivation paths rather than letting elegant slogans win.
summary: The satisfaction comes from clashing convictions, not modern motivational advice.
details: Establish the opponent's reasoning, find its internal contradiction, then answer through the protagonist's lived experience.
applicable_scenes: Debates on the Way|scriptural disputes|sect contests|mentor-student arguments
pitfalls: Empty preaching|modern inspirational slogans|straw-man opponents
positive_example: He does not deny the path of detachment. He asks why its elder has kept a lamp burning for a dead disciple for thirty years.
negative_example: He says everyone should be themselves, and every cultivator instantly attains enlightenment.

intent_synonyms: how to write magical contracts|supernatural intimacy|spirit companions
model_instruction: Let contracts, bloodlines, spiritual objects and clan law continually affect intimacy.
summary: Supernatural romance works when its rules both protect and wound.
details: Express feeling through contract marks' warmth, unstable energy, clan responses and unequal lifespans rather than cosmetic magic.
pitfalls: Lore exists only for rescues|taboos lack consequences|one-use magical details
positive_example: She insists it does not hurt, but the mark on her wrist darkens like dead ash and even the gate's spirit crane retreats.
negative_example: Divine and demonic lovers follow an ordinary television romance with only their titles changed.

intent_synonyms: how to change canon|manage butterfly effects
model_instruction: Show direct consequences and long-term ripples; saving a person must change the world.
summary: Fresh fanfiction follows altered canon events toward a newly coherent central conflict.
details: Every intervention should trigger enemy reactions, faction shifts and new threats.
applicable_scenes: Saving doomed characters|alternate timelines|rewritten chronology|original-character intervention
pitfalls: Changes have no consequences|copying canon unchanged|uncontrolled narrative drift
positive_example: The day after he saves the man, an antagonist who should have remained silent issues an early challenge.
negative_example: The protagonist changes a major battle, but every later event proceeds exactly as in canon.

keywords: mechanics literacy|cooldown windows|team voice chat|tactical counters
intent_synonyms: how to write game combat|explain raid mechanics
model_instruction: Show how mechanics are interpreted so victory does not feel arbitrary.
summary: Readable combat depends on ability windows, position changes, resource exchanges and team roles.
details: Use one or two decisive mechanics in a team fight rather than filling the screen with ability names.
pitfalls: Ability-name bombardment|rules changed mid-fight|teammates merely cheer
positive_example: During the healer's half-second cast, he deliberately holds his movement skill, waiting for the opposing assassin to reveal himself.
negative_example: Effects fill the screen, everyone uses their abilities, and the protagonist wins.

intent_synonyms: how to write family disputes|village confrontations
model_instruction: Ground kinship conflict in reputation, resources and elder authority rather than mere tantrums.
summary: The payoff comes from commanding reason, evidence and community opinion in a close-knit society.
details: Give relatives concrete methods of exploitation and give the protagonist a public exposure opportunity plus lasting boundaries.
pitfalls: Villains only scream|endless protagonist submission|no relational aftermath
positive_example: She does not argue. She opens the grain-loan ledger in the ancestral hall and asks the senior uncle to read the first entry.
negative_example: A relative insults the protagonist, who insults them back and immediately earns the entire village's admiration.

intent_synonyms: how to write period workplaces|factory relationships|competition for places
model_instruction: Show allocations, evaluations, apprenticeships and collective opinion; do not turn the factory into a modern corporation.
summary: A work unit controls wages, housing, honors and introduction letters, all capable of changing lives.
details: Center conflict on who may sign, who dares testify and who risks losing recognition.
pitfalls: Modern corporate jargon|vague authority|collective evaluations have no effects
positive_example: The workshop director does not scold him; he simply moves his name off the honors list, and the room goes quiet.
negative_example: The boss announces KPIs and the workers launch into modern corporate competition.

intent_synonyms: how to preserve canon speech|use catchphrases sparingly
model_instruction: Build voice from syntax, values and response timing; catchphrases are only accents.
summary: Repeating a famous line does not reproduce the person; judgment under pressure matters more.
details: Check diction, sentence length, emotional openness, address habits and consistency with canonical relationships.
applicable_scenes: Canon characters meeting|romantic pairings|pre-battle dialogue|daily-life extras
pitfalls: Too many catchphrases|identical voices|personality rewritten for convenience
positive_example: He stops halfway through a sentence, calculates the debt first, then decides whether to offer a rescue.
negative_example: A reserved character suddenly makes a stream of cute jokes as though replaced by someone else.

intent_synonyms: how to write historical case files|court evidence|appeal documents
model_instruction: Ground a historical appeal in documents, witnesses and precedent rather than a single declaration of truth.
summary: Credibility comes from the evidence chain, not the protagonist's aura of insight.
details: Statements, seals, ledgers, old judgments and witness status must interlock; missing links leave risk.
pitfalls: Evidence appears from nowhere|spoken deduction replaces records|precedents are decoration
positive_example: Instead of protesting innocence, he asks the magistrate to compare the red seal with the seam stamp on a five-year-old grain ledger.
negative_example: The protagonist states the truth and everyone immediately believes it.

intent_synonyms: how to write gentle gratification|show life getting better
model_instruction: Turn each gain into changed daily life instead of simply increasing numbers.
summary: Small possessions and habits make accumulated improvement feel secure and real.
details: A hot meal, thick blanket, oil lamp or reliable customer can mark progress.
pitfalls: Only income totals|unchanged daily detail|nobody reacts to improvement
positive_example: Her sister touches the new quilt three times as it dries in the yard, then quietly asks whether they can go to bed early.
negative_example: Income doubles but living conditions and family attitudes remain exactly the same.

intent_synonyms: how to introduce missions concisely|world transitions
model_instruction: Present the dilemma before the rules so system exposition does not stall the opening.
summary: A fast arc still needs readers to understand who owes what to whom.
details: Combine immediate danger, fragments of the original person's memory and one crucial system line instead of a full lecture.
pitfalls: Overlong lore|vague objectives|undefined original grievances
positive_example: She hears a cup shatter before memory reveals that the engagement banquet was arranged to humiliate her.
negative_example: The system spends two thousand words explaining the world and every relationship.

keywords: supernatural senses|energy resonance|shared contract pain|nonhuman viewpoint
intent_synonyms: how to describe magical perception|divine and demonic senses
model_instruction: Connect perception to species, energy and contracts rather than adding mystical adjectives to ordinary senses.
summary: A nonhuman viewpoint is compelling because it perceives the world differently.
details: Demons may smell emotion, gods sense vows, bonded partners share pain and spirits detect danger before humans.
pitfalls: Ordinary senses with new labels|energy only glows|nonhumans perceive exactly like humans
positive_example: She cannot hear lies, but she can smell the cold trace of an oath at the end of his words.
negative_example: She admires pretty spiritual energy, then the pair resumes an otherwise ordinary romance.

intent_synonyms: how to make magical duels clear|show energy costs
model_instruction: Clarify spell functions, counters and expenditure instead of exploding named techniques across the page.
summary: The payoff comes when readers understand why a particular spell breaks the deadlock.
details: Remaining energy, casting range, artifact capacity, elemental counters and local energy can establish combat logic.
pitfalls: Technique-name lists|infinite energy|new counters invented on demand
positive_example: Rather than blocking the fire-crow talisman, he cuts the water vein beside the formation's core, reducing the enemy's flames by a third.
negative_example: Both sides shout technique names; light explodes, and the protagonist wins.

intent_synonyms: how to use canonical references|avoid awkward homage
model_instruction: Use a few precise callbacks aimed at the emotional core of a character or famous scene, not a barrage of references.
summary: Fan service should create recognition without turning the story into a list of memes.
details: Old lines, props and settings belong where emotion aligns, and their appearance should advance the current scene.
applicable_scenes: Variations on famous scenes|first meetings|romantic extras|ending echoes
pitfalls: Reference overload|jokes break atmosphere|homage does not move the plot
positive_example: He stops where the famous line would have continued. Without hearing it all, readers know whom he remembers.
negative_example: Characters quote one canonical meme after another until the story resembles a comment compilation.

keywords: period colloquial speech|neighborly greetings|indirect expression|collective language
intent_synonyms: how to write natural historical dialogue|avoid modern phrasing
model_instruction: Organize speech around work roles, coupons, reputation and collective expectations rather than modern emotional jargon.
summary: Period voice is not forced dialect; speakers assume the workplace and neighborhood are socially present.
details: Greetings may circle around supplies, criticism invoke collective judgment, and grievances preserve face.
pitfalls: Modern internet phrases|excessive dialect|everyone states private feelings directly
positive_example: She does not say she feels wronged. She asks whether the half-pound cooking-oil coupon was also allocated by the collective.
negative_example: She says she is emotionally burned out and everyone has terrible boundaries.

keywords: domestic intrigue subtext|ritual barbs|changing address|polite conflict
intent_synonyms: how to write household intrigue|historical sarcasm|ritual conflict
model_instruction: Hide attacks inside courtesy instead of staging a modern public shouting match.
summary: Restraint in formal settings makes the implied wound sharper.
details: Forms of address, seating, gifts and polite phrases can all function as weapons.
applicable_scenes: Family banquets|formal greetings|arranged marriages|household power struggles
pitfalls: Public screaming|ritual has no function|subtext explicitly explained
positive_example: She smiles and calls her “elder sister,” while placing the teacup firmly at the lower-ranked seat.
negative_example: She publicly calls her rival manipulative and everyone applauds.
